###### Abstract
We introduce a novel parametrization of the correlation matrix.  This parametrization can be viewed as a generalization of Fisher’s Z-transformation to higher dimensions and has a wide range of potential applications. An algorithm for reconstructing the unique n×n correlation matrix from any vector in ℝ^(n(n-1)/2) is provided, and we derive its numerical complexity.
## 1 Introduction
It is convenient to reparametrize a covariance matrix as a vector that is unrestricted in ℝ^d, and the literature has proposed several methods to this end, see Pinheiro & Bates (1996). These methods include the Cholesky decomposition, the spherical trigonometric transformation, transformations based on partial correlation vines, and methods based on the spectral representation, such as the matrix logarithm, see e.g. Kurowicka & Cooke (2003).
We do not apply the matrix logarithm to covariance matrices, but to correlation matrices. Modeling the correlation matrix separately from the individual variances is commonly done in multivariate GARCH models, see e.g. Bollerslev (1990), Engle (2002), Tse & Tsui (2002), and Engle & Kelly (2012). The new parametrization can be used to define a new family of multivariate GARCH models, that need not impose additional restrictions beyond positivity.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6853692/)Abstract

### Motivation

High throughput technologies are widely employed in modern biomedical research. They yield measurements of a large number of biomolecules in a single experiment. The number of experiments usually is much smaller than the number of measurements in each experiment. The simultaneous measurements of biomolecules provide a basis for a comprehensive, systems view for describing relevant biological processes. Often it is necessary to determine correlations between the data matrices under different conditions or pathways. However, the techniques for analyzing the data with a low number of samples for possible correlations within or between conditions are still in development. Earlier developed correlative measures, such as the RV coefficient, use the trace of the product of data matrices as the most relevant characteristic. However, a recent study has shown that the RV coefficient consistently overestimates the correlations in the case of low sample numbers. To correct for this bias, it was suggested to discard the diagonal elements of the outer products of each data matrix. In this work, a principled approach based on the matrix decomposition generates three trace-independent parts for every matrix. These components are unique, and they are used to determine different aspects of correlations between the original datasets.

### Results

Simulations show that the decomposition results in the removal of high correlation bias and the dependence on the sample number intrinsic to the RV coefficient. We then use the correlations to analyze a real proteomics dataset.

###### Abstract

Solving sparse linear systems is a critical challenge in many scientific and engineering fields, particularly when these systems are severely ill-conditioned. This work aims to provide a comprehensive comparison of various solvers designed for such problems, offering valuable insights and guidance for domain scientists and researchers. We develop the tools required to accurately evaluate the performance and correctness of 16 solvers from 11 state-of-the-art numerical libraries, focusing on their effectiveness in handling ill-conditioned matrices. The solvers were tested on linear systems arising from a coupled hydro-mechanical marker-in-cell geophysical simulation. keenable.title: A variational approach to the generalized Fisher transformation of correlation matrices
keenable.snippet: > Abstract:The generalized Fisher transformation maps a non-singular correlation matrix to an unconstrained real vector through the off-diagonal elements of its matrix logarithm. We show that the inverse transformation is the unique minimizer of a smooth, strictly convex and coercive function of the diagonal elements of the matrix logarithm, which yields a new and short proof that the transformation is one-to-one and onto. The Hessian of this function is bounded, at every point, between the extreme eigenvalues of the associated matrix exponential and is dominated by the diagonal of that exponential, a bound that is attained. These bounds identify the standard fixed-point iteration for the inverse as a quasi-Newton method whose worst-case local factor can approach one for near-singular correlation matrices, and guarantee that the Newton system is never worse conditioned than the matrix exponential. We propose GFT-FP+N, which augments the fixed-point iteration with matrix-free Newton steps computed by conjugate gradients, with no explicit Jacobian. In benchmark experiments GFT-FP+N converged in all tested instances, including instances in which Broyden's method failed, and reduced computation time by up to a factor of thirty relative to the fixed-point iteration.

keenable.title: Fast inversion of the generalized Fisher transformation of correlation matrices
keenable.snippet: The generalized Fisher transformation maps a non-singular correlation matrix to an unconstrained real vector through the off-diagonal elements of its matrix logarithm. Evaluating its inverse is a computational bottleneck in dynamic correlation and multivariate volatility models. We develop a fast inversion algorithm by characterizing the unknown diagonal as the minimizer of a smooth, strictly convex, and coercive objective. An explicit Hessian and global spectral bounds identify the standard fixed-point iteration as a quasi-Newton method and explain why it can converge slowly near singularity. Every fixed-point step decreases the objective, and the iteration converges from every starting point. These results motivate GFT-FP+N, a hybrid of fixed-point and matrix-free Newton steps that never forms the Jacobian. In benchmarks with up to 1,000 replications per design and dimensions up to 800, GFT-FP+N reduces computation time by up to a factor of forty-five relative to the fixed-point iteration and converged in every replication, including on designs where Broyden's method almost always fails.

We introduce the *balanced correlation parametrization* (BCP), which maps positive-definite correlation matrices one-to-one onto the set of symmetric hollow matrices. A key feature of the parametrization is that both the transformation and its inverse are available in closed form. A novel property of BCP is that it preserves correlation sparsity as the dimension tends to infinity under suitable factor conditions, providing a basis for sparse high-dimensional correlation modeling. An empirical illustration using standardized idiosyncratic daily stock returns for 1,765 equities over 15 years shows that BCP retains the approximate sparsity pattern and magnitudes of shock correlations, and that it yields accurate positive-definite reconstructions under sparse coordinate restrictions.

Title: Fast inversion of the generalized Fisher transformation of correlation matrices

Authors: Ilya Archakov, Peter Reinhard Hansen

View PDF HTML (experimental)

Abstract: The generalized Fisher transformation maps a non-singular correlation matrix to an unconstrained real vector through the off-diagonal elements of its matrix logarithm. Evaluating its inverse is a computational bottleneck in dynamic correlation and multivariate volatility models. We develop a fast inversion algorithm by characterizing the unknown diagonal as the minimizer of a smooth, strictly convex, and coercive objective. An explicit Hessian and global spectral bounds identify the standard fixed-point iteration as a quasi-Newton method and explain why it can converge slowly near singularity. Every fixed-point step decreases the objective, and the iteration converges from every starting point. These results motivate GFT-FP+N, a hybrid of fixed-point and matrix-free Newton steps that never forms the Jacobian. In benchmarks with up to 1,000 replications per design and dimensions up to 800, GFT-FP+N reduces computation time by up to a factor of forty-five relative to the fixed-point iteration and converged in every replication, including on designs where Broyden's method almost always fails. Julia and R packages are provided.

octen.title: An Iterative Block Matrix Inversion (IBMI) Algorithm for Symmetric Positive Definite Matrices with Applications to Covariance Matrices
octen.snippet: Obtaining the inverse of a large symmetric positive definite matrix $\mathcal{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times p}$ is a continual challenge across many mathematical disciplines. In this paper, we present a novel iterative algorithm (IBMI), which is designed to approximate the inverse of a large, dense, symmetric positive definite matrix. Abstract

In a wide range of applications it is required to compute the nearest correlation matrix in the Frobenius norm to a given symmetric but indefinite matrix. Of the available methods with guaranteed convergence to the unique solution of this problem the easiest to implement, and perhaps the most widely used, is the alternating projections method. However, the rate of convergence of this method is at best linear, and it can require a large number of iterations to converge to within a given tolerance. We show that Anderson acceleration, a technique for accelerating the convergence of fixed-point iterations, can be applied to the alternating projections method and that in practice it brings a significant reduction in both the number of iterations and the computation time. We also show that Anderson acceleration remains effective, and indeed can provide even greater improvements, when it is applied to the variants of the nearest correlation matrix problem in which specified elements are fixed or a lower bound is imposed on the smallest eigenvalue. Alternating projections is a general method for finding a point in the intersection of several sets and ours appears to be the first demonstration that this class of methods can benefit from Anderson acceleration.

Abstract
The generalized Fisher transformation maps a non-singular correlation matrix to an un- constrained real vector through the off-diagonal elements of its matrix logarithm. ## Positive-Definite Covariance Matrix Construction

Most risk teams meet positive definiteness as a failure. A Monte Carlo engine refuses to run because a Cholesky factorisation hit a negative number, a stress scenario produces a negative portfolio variance, or an optimiser returns weights that make no sense. The usual response is repair: clip the negative eigenvalues, find the nearest valid matrix, shrink towards something safe. That toolkit is covered in Correlation Matrices and Positive Semidefiniteness, and this article does not repeat it. The question here is different: **how do you build a covariance or correlation matrix so that an invalid one is impossible in the first place?**

Repair has a hidden cost: it moves numbers you chose on purpose. If a scenario designer sets the equity–credit correlation to −0.9 and a nearest-matrix routine quietly softens it, the stress that was signed off is not the stress that was run. ## Correlation Matrix Construction for Market Models

A LIBOR or forward market model needs one number for every pair of forward rates: how strongly their shocks move together. With 19 annual forwards that is 171 correlations, and together they decide how the model prices every swaption, spread option and Bermudan in the book. Nobody hands you those 171 numbers. You estimate them from noisy data, and the estimate is usually not fit to use as it stands. This post is about the step between the estimate and the model: building a correlation matrix that is valid, smooth and close to the truth. It then measures, against a truth we know, which construction wins and what the choice does to swaption prices.

## 1. Why a Market Model Needs a Built Correlation Matrix

In the lognormal market model each forward Fi follows d*F*i/*F*i = σi(*t*) d*W*i plus a measure-dependent drift, with d⟨*W*i, *W*j⟩ = ρij d*t* (the set-up is in LIBOR Market Model Fundamentals). The matrix ρ has to meet three demands at once:

- **Validity.** It must be positive semidefinite (PSD) with ones on the diagonal, or the Cholesky factor that drives the simulation does not exist and some portfolio of forwards has negative variance. Correlation Matrices and Positive Semidefiniteness covers why.
- **Plausible shape.** Correlation should fall as the gap between two maturities grows, and ideally flatten out at long gaps. The parametric forms that deliver this are compared in Correlation Structures in Forward Rate Models.
- **Accuracy.** It should be close to the true co-movement, because swaption prices depend on it and caplet prices do not.

A raw sample estimate only reliably meets the third demand, and only roughly.

How to repair a non-positive-definite stressed correlation matrix with eigenvalue clipping, Higham's nearest correlation matrix in numpy and shrinkage, and what each repair does to your stressed correlations and VaR.

## Repairing Non-Positive-Definite Covariance Matrices

## 1. When a Stressed Matrix Stops Being a Matrix

A stress tester sits down with a perfectly healthy correlation matrix estimated from history and starts overwriting entries. Equity and high-yield credit will move together almost one for one in the scenario, so that pair goes to 0.95. Stocks and government bonds will sell off together, as they do when inflation rather than growth is the worry, so that pair goes from negative to +0.50. Everything else is left as it was. The numbers are each defensible. Then the risk engine refuses to run: the Cholesky factorization fails, the Monte Carlo simulation cannot draw correlated shocks, and a portfolio variance somewhere comes out negative.

The matrix has stopped being a correlation matrix. Why that happens, and why hand-edited and pairwise-estimated matrices are especially prone to it, is the subject of Correlation Matrices and Positive Definiteness; in one sentence, the entries are not free numbers but must be jointly consistent, and editing two of them can break that consistency even when each is plausible on its own. This post is about what happens next: the repair.

There are three standard repairs, and every one of them returns a valid matrix. What is rarely discussed is that they return *different* valid matrices, and that each one quietly rewrites the correlations you set on purpose. A stress scenario is a deliberate statement about the world. A repair that pulls 0.95 back to 0.81 has changed that statement, and the change shows up in the VaR. The repair is a modelling choice with a cost, and the cost can be measured. That is what we will do, on one broken 4×4 matrix, with code you can run.

## Cholesky Decomposition for Correlated Risk Factors

Most textbook options depend on one stock. Many real ones depend on several: a basket call on three shares, a worst-of note, a portfolio whose Value at Risk mixes equities, rates and currencies. The moment two or more risk factors enter one price, you need them to move together the way they do in the market, with the right correlation, and a random number generator only gives you independent draws. Cholesky decomposition is the small piece of linear algebra that turns independent draws into correlated ones. This post does it by hand on three illustrative stocks, checks it by simulation, prices a basket call with it, and then walks through the two ways it goes wrong in practice.

## 1. Why a Basket Call Needs Correlated Risk Factors

A basket call pays the average of several share prices minus a strike, if that is positive, at expiry. Its value depends heavily on how the shares move together. If they tend to rise and fall together, the average swings almost as much as each share, and the option is valuable. If they move independently, their ups and downs partly cancel inside the average, the basket is calmer, and the option is cheaper. So the correlation between the risk factors is not a detail; it is a price input on the same footing as volatility.

A Monte Carlo pricer needs, on every simulated path, one random shock per stock, and those shocks must have the correlations you believe in. A computer can produce standard normal draws, written *z*: numbers with mean 0 and variance 1, each independent of the others. The job is a recipe that mixes independent *z*'s into correlated shocks, written *ε* (epsilon).

If you profiled the linear algebra running inside a bank's risk engine tonight, one factorisation would dominate the trace: Cholesky. Every Monte Carlo VaR run that needs correlated asset returns calls it. Every multivariate normal likelihood evaluation calls it. Every Mahalanobis distance computed against a covariance matrix calls it. It is the most-used matrix factorisation in quantitative finance, and the reason is that it is the natural factorisation of exactly the object finance cares most about: the covariance matrix.

## 1. What Cholesky Decomposition Actually Is

Cholesky decomposition writes a symmetric positive definite matrix $\mathbf{A}$ as the product of a lower triangular matrix and its own transpose:

$$\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{L}\mathbf{L}^\top$$

Cholesky throws away that independence: because $\mathbf{A}$ is symmetric, the upper factor is already determined by the lower one, so there is nothing to compute twice.

ultimate.title: A variational approach to the generalized Fisher transformation of correlation matrices
ultimate.snippet: > Abstract:The generalized Fisher transformation maps a non-singular correlation matrix to an unconstrained real vector through the off-diagonal elements of its matrix logarithm. We show that the inverse transformation is the unique minimizer of a smooth, strictly convex and coercive function of the diagonal elements of the matrix logarithm, which yields a new and short proof that the transformation is one-to-one and onto. The Hessian of this function is bounded, at every point, between the extreme eigenvalues of the associated matrix exponential and is dominated by the diagonal of that exponential, a bound that is attained. These bounds identify the standard fixed-point iteration for the inverse as a quasi-Newton method whose worst-case local factor can approach one for near-singular correlation matrices, and guarantee that the Newton system is never worse conditioned than the matrix exponential. We propose GFT-FP+N, which augments the fixed-point iteration with matrix-free Newton steps computed by conjugate gradients, with no explicit Jacobian. In benchmark experiments GFT-FP+N converged in all tested instances, including instances in which Broyden's method failed, and reduced computation time by up to a factor of thirty relative to the fixed-point iteration.

ultimate.snippet: The generalized Fisher transformation maps a non-singular correlation matrix to an unconstrained real vector through the off-diagonal elements of its matrix logarithm. Evaluating its inverse is a computational bottleneck in dynamic correlation and multivariate volatility models. We develop a fast inversion algorithm by characterizing the unknown diagonal as the minimizer of a smooth, strictly convex, and coercive objective. In this paper, we propose an alternative Cholesky block decomposition (ACBD) for the covariance matrix of multivariate longitudinal data. The new unconstrained parameterization is capable to automatically eliminate the positive definiteness constraint of the covariance matrix and robustly estimate the correlation matrix with respect to the model misspecifications of the nested prediction error covariance matrices.
In this paper, we propose a multivariate t regression model with its mean and scale covariance modeled jointly for the analysis of longitudinal data. A modified Cholesky decomposition is adopted to factorize the dependence structure in terms of unconstrained autoregressive and scale innovation parameters.
It was shown that the estimators for the parametric parts in both the mean and covariance are consistent and asymptotically normally distributed, and the nonparametric parts could be estimated at an optimal rate of convergence Simulation studies and real data analysis illustrate that the proposed approach could yield highly reliable estimation of the mean and covariance matrix.Read more
We propose a longitudinal principal component analysis method for multivariate longitudinal data using a random-effects eigen-decomposition, where the eigen-decomposition utilizes longitudinal information through nonparametric splines and the multivariate random effects incorporate significant store-wise heterogeneity. Our method can effectively analyze large marketing data containing sales information for products from hundreds of stores over an 11-year time period. The proposed method leads to more accurate estimation and interpretation compared to existing approaches.

you.title: Restoring Definiteness via Shrinking, with an Application to ...
you.snippet:
Indefinite approximations of positive semidefinite matrices arise in various data analysis applications involving covariance matrices and correlation matrices. We propose a method for restoring positive semidefiniteness of an indefinite matrix $M_0$ that constructs a convex linear combination $S(\alpha) = \alpha M_1 + (1-\alpha)M_0$ of $M_0$ and a positive semidefinite target matrix $M_1$. In statistics, this construction for improving an estimate $M_0$ by combining it with new information in $M_1$ is known as shrinking.
